title: Spondylolisthesis
intro: Spondylolisthesis occurs when one vertebra slips forward over the one beneath it, most often in the lower back. It may cause back pain, leg pain or no symptoms at all. Degenerative spondylolisthesis typically affects older adults. Most people improve with exercise and activity changes, and surgery is for a minority.

sections.heading: Types and causes
paragraphs: In older people, degenerative slippage results from wear of discs and facet joints, often at the fourth and fifth lumbar vertebrae. In younger people, a stress fracture of part of the vertebra, often in athletes such as gymnasts and football players, can allow slippage. Rare causes include injury, birth differences and tumours.

sections.heading: Symptoms
paragraphs: Symptoms include lower back pain that worsens with standing or extending the spine, stiffness, tight hamstrings, and sometimes pain, numbness or weakness in the legs from nerve irritation, similar to spinal stenosis. Some people notice a change in posture or walk. Many people with slippage have no pain.

sections.heading: Diagnosis
paragraphs: Doctors examine and request standing X-rays that show the slippage and grade it by percentage. MRI or CT scans show nerve compression or bone defects. Imaging findings do not always match the severity of pain.

sections.heading: Treatment
paragraphs: Initial treatment includes avoiding activities that provoke pain, short-term painkillers and physiotherapy to strengthen core and back muscles. Young athletes may need rest from sport and sometimes a brace. Epidural injections may help leg symptoms. Most people improve over weeks to months.

Surgery, including decompression and fusion of the vertebrae, is considered when severe or worsening nerve symptoms, instability or persistent pain remain after conservative treatment, or when slippage is large. Recovery takes months.

sections.heading: Monitoring and prevention
paragraphs: Slippage seldom progresses in adults. Children and teenagers with slippage need follow-up during growth. Maintain strong core muscles, keep a healthy weight and take caution with high-impact repetitive back extension activities. Report new leg weakness or bladder or bowel changes right away.

examples.title: Adjusting sport
examples.text: Imagine your teenager has back pain from gymnastics and slippage on an X-ray. You could discuss rest from the sport, physiotherapy and follow-up scans with the doctor.

examples.title: Strengthening
examples.text: Suppose you have back pain when standing. You might start core stabilisation exercises with a physiotherapist and avoid long periods of standing without a break.
